16892:
Choose a cable

A ready-made RC5 SRS adapter is optional. You can build a dedicated 16-pin OBD extension if the documented vehicle pinout applies.

Mini MPI wiring

MEMS 2J engine K-line uses OBD pin 7; RC5/EC5 airbag SRS diagnosis uses OBD pin 13. Detecting a USB COM port is not proof of communication with the SRS ECU.

Build the extension

1. Unplug both USB and vehicle ends. 2. Identify moulded pin numbers on the connectors, checking whether you see the front or rear view. 3. Route KKL tool-side pin 7 (K output) to vehicle-side OBD pin 13 on a cable dedicated to RC5. 4. Do NOT permanently bridge vehicle pins 7 and 13. 5. With a meter, check continuity tool 7 → vehicle 13 and the absence of shorts or any link between the two vehicle diagnostic circuits. 6. Clearly label RC5 SRS.

Limits

Do not alter car wiring, airbags or pretensioners. On JDM Mini, MGF, MG TF or other Rover variants, verify the exact vehicle diagram: this mapping is not universal. Test on an actual RC5 unit remains necessary.

Sources

pscan.uk/features/mini.html; RoverMEMS RC5 documentation; SESSION research report 22.
16894:
Make it yourself or obtain a prepared cable

A Lucas 5AS-compatible diagnostic lead can be made from a suitable VAG-COM KKL 409.1 with a genuine FT232R or compatible CH340G, plus a removable OBD extension. A standard engine lead is NOT directly compatible.

Step 1A — genuine FTDI FT232R

Unplug from the vehicle. In FT_PROG on the PC select DEVICES → Scan & Parse; identify the right FT232R; select Hardware Specific → Invert RS232 Signals → Invert RXD; choose DEVICES → Program. Unplug/replug USB to reload settings, then read back the configuration. Many counterfeit FT232R chips cannot store this setting.

Alternative step 1B — CH340G solder modification

Unplug everything and open the KKL housing. Confirm the IC really is a 16-pin CH340G, identify the pin-1 notch/dot and check the board. On the design illustrated by Andrew Revill, if CH340G IC pin 15 (R232) is unconnected, bridge CHIP pin 15 to CHIP pin 16 (VCC) to enable inverted RXD. If pin 15 already carries a track, do not bridge blindly: the PCB may require a specialist modification. Inspect solder joints with power removed. These are the IC pins, NOT OBD connector pins 15 and 16! Do not apply this procedure indiscriminately to CH340C/CH341.

Step 2 — remap a detachable OBD extension

The normal KKL transmits on OBD 7 (K) and receives on 15 (L). A 5AS vehicle with a 16-pin socket receives tool commands on OBD 3 (module C61-16) and sends its inverted reply on OBD 1 (module C61-24). On the extension OUTLET dedicated to 5AS, exchange contacts 3 ↔ 7 and 1 ↔ 15. A single extension is enough; a two-port splitter is optional. Keep a separate engine outlet straight-through.

Step 3 — check the finished lead

With power disconnected, check continuity from KKL-side 7 → vehicle-side 3 and KKL-side 15 ← vehicle-side 1. Check for unintended bridges. Leave the correct supply and ground wiring intact and label the cable 5AS, distinct from the engine KKL. RXD signal inversion and OBD contact swapping are TWO independent changes.

Voltage and other sockets

The 5AS uses approximately 0–12 V automotive levels and inverted transmit: never wire a bare 3.3/5 V TTL adapter or desktop RS-232 directly to the vehicle. Some older Minis have a green three-pin 5AS socket; its pinout differs and must be checked against the exact vehicle wiring diagram. COM detection alone never proves a successful 5AS connection.

16896:
Lucas 5AS PLIP remote learning

The key-programming module will use the SAME adapted 5AS diagnostic cable as the immobiliser reader: genuine FT232R or compatible CH340G KKL with inverted RXD and, on 16-pin vehicles, routing KKL pin 7 → vehicle 3 and KKL pin 15 ← vehicle 1.

No purchase required

To build a cable, follow the full DIY procedure under the Immobiliser column’s Cable information button, including chip identification, the required RXD change, OBD extension contact remapping, meter checks and labelling. A prepared lead is an alternative, not a requirement.

Radio frequency is different

433.92 MHz or 315 MHz describes the remote’s radio, not the diagnostic cable. A garage remote at 433 MHz is not necessarily compatible. A Lucas 5AS learning operation may replace the remotes previously paired.

Other modules

Pektron SCU and Lucas 10AS are different families. No universally verified DIY cable pinout for Manager is available yet. Do not copy the 5AS scheme to them without the exact vehicle evidence. Key programming is not active yet.
